notes: Seventeen elements are generally classed as essential for higher plants. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come largely from air and water; the other fourteen are mineral nutrients. Macronutrient/micronutrient describes amount needed, not importance. Nitrogen supports proteins and chlorophyll, phosphorus energy-transfer compounds, potassium enzyme activity and osmotic regulation. Do not describe potassium as a structural protein component. Visual symptoms alone are not a diagnosis.

Limestone neutralizes soil acidity; a dose cannot be selected from pH alone. Gypsum supplies calcium and sulfur without a net liming effect. Do not prescribe gypsum as a general product for lowering high pH or for fixing every clay soil. High pH, salinity and sodicity are different conditions and need appropriate measurements. Compost or management can improve structure and water relations without changing the mineral particle-size class.

Electrical conductivity interpretation depends on how the extract was prepared. Do not equate irrigation-water EC, saturation-extract ECe and other soil-water-ratio readings. Salinity is soluble salt stress; sodicity concerns sodium in relation to exchange properties. Leaching requires suitable water and effective drainage; it is not a universal prescription. Do not convert a field appearance or an unspecified EC measurement directly into a treatment dose.

Plant-available water is conventionally the water between field capacity and permanent wilting point. Soil texture affects water retention, but very tightly held water is not readily available. Effective root depth and structure matter. Do not infer a universal irrigation interval from clay content or use visible wilting as the sole scheduling trigger. All example calculations must be explicitly simulated and dimensionally consistent.
